reading.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions.
reading.text: Urban farming — growing food inside cities — is becoming more common in many African countries. In Accra, Nairobi and Yaoundé, families grow vegetables on rooftops, in small gardens and even along roadsides. Supporters say that urban farming provides fresh food, creates jobs for young people and reduces the cost of transporting food from rural areas. However, it also faces problems. Land in cities is expensive, and many farmers do not have legal permission to use the land they cultivate. In addition, the water used for irrigation is sometimes polluted, which can make vegetables unsafe to eat. Some city councils have started to support urban farmers by giving them training and access to clean water. Experts believe that, if these problems are solved, urban farming could feed a significant part of the growing urban population.

reading.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions.
reading.text: For decades, sleep was regarded as a passive state in which the brain simply rested. Research over the past thirty years has overturned this view. During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay the experiences of the day, strengthening the connections that form long-term memories. In one widely cited experiment, students who slept after learning a list of words remembered significantly more of them the next day than students who stayed awake for the same period. Interestingly, the benefit was greatest for the information the students had found most difficult. Not all researchers agree on how these results should be interpreted. Some argue that sleep actively consolidates memory; others suggest that it merely protects new memories from interference by reducing the amount of new information the brain receives. What is clear, however, is that the common student habit of sacrificing sleep to study all night may be counterproductive.

reading.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions.
reading.text: Predictions that automation would make human labour obsolete are almost as old as industrial machinery itself. Each wave of technology has, nevertheless, created more jobs than it destroyed — though rarely for the same people, and seldom in the same places. The current debate about artificial intelligence differs in one important respect: previous machines replaced physical effort, whereas AI encroaches on cognitive tasks once thought to be uniquely human. Optimists contend that, freed from routine analysis, workers will move towards activities requiring judgement, empathy and creativity. Sceptics counter that such a transition presupposes large-scale retraining, which neither governments nor employers have historically funded adequately. The outcome, in other words, may depend less on the technology itself than on institutional choices. To frame the question as "Will machines take our jobs?" is therefore to misplace the emphasis; the more pressing question is who will bear the cost of adaptation.
